blocks.text: **Adhesive capsulitis**, or **frozen shoulder**, is a condition in which the shoulder becomes painful and stiff, and passive range is clearly reduced in a typical pattern. The joint capsule is thought to become inflamed and thickened [Ref - to verify]. The exact cause is not fully understood.

It is more common between about 40 and 60 years old and is reported more often in women [Ref - to verify]. It is linked with diabetes, thyroid disease and some other conditions [Ref - to verify]. **Primary** frozen shoulder has no clear cause; **secondary** follows an injury, surgery or immobilisation.
The course is often described in phases, although the boundaries are not sharp [Ref - to verify]:

rows: Increasing pain, often worse at night, progressive loss of movement
Pain eases, stiffness is the main problem

blocks.text: The whole course can last many months to a few years, and some patients keep some stiffness [Ref - to verify].

items: Gradual onset of shoulder pain, often severe and at night, with growing stiffness.
Difficulty combing hair, reaching behind the back, fastening a bra, reaching a seat belt.
Both active and **passive** movement are limited, with external rotation usually the most affected, then abduction and internal rotation (a capsular pattern).
The end of range feels firm and painful, not just painful.

rows: When did it start and how fast did stiffness grow?
Is night pain a major problem?
Any injury, surgery or arm immobilisation?
Diabetes, thyroid disease, cardiac or lung disease?
Which movements do you lose most?
Any previous dislocation, fall or arthritis?
Any weight loss, constant pain, fever?

items: Observation of posture, muscle bulk and scapular movement.
Active range: elevation, external rotation, internal rotation (hand behind back).
**Passive range** compared with the other side, especially external rotation with the arm at the side.
End-feel and irritability.
Resisted tests (strength usually appears normal apart from pain).
Cervical screen and neurological screen.
General health screen if there are systemic features.

blocks.text: E1. Passive external rotation at the side

rows: Identify the key sign of frozen shoulder: large loss of passive external rotation
Supine or sitting, elbow at the side bent to 90 degrees
Beside the patient, one hand stabilising the elbow, the other holding the wrist
Rotate the forearm outward slowly until firm resistance or pain stops it; use a goniometer if available; compare with the other side

Clearly reduced passive external rotation compared with the other side, often with a firm end-feel. Some classification criteria use a loss of at least 50% of the other side [Ref - to verify exact criteria]
Passive external rotation approximately equal to the other side
Supports adhesive capsulitis, especially if other directions are also limited
Also reduced in glenohumeral osteoarthritis and some dislocations; a normal X-ray helps separate them
Allowing trunk lean or shoulder shrug; not stabilising the elbow; forcing past the end-feel
If positive, check passive abduction and internal rotation, and refer for X-ray if arthritis or locked dislocation is possible

blocks.text: E2. Passive abduction and internal rotation

Measure passive abduction (with scapular stabilisation to avoid substituting scapular motion) and hand-behind-back reach. Loss in several directions, with external rotation most affected, supports the capsular pattern.
E3. Active versus passive comparison
In RCRSP, passive range is usually close to normal while active range is limited by pain. In frozen shoulder both are limited. This comparison is the quickest clinical separation.

rows: Older age, grinding, joint space loss on X-ray
Recent seizure, electric shock or fall; external rotation severely blocked
Sudden severe pain, calcification on X-ray

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Stiff shoulder after a seizure, electric shock or high-energy fall, with severely reduced external rotation
Joint locked in the wrong position
Do not mobilise; refer for imaging
Constant severe night pain with weight loss, cancer history
Bilateral stiffness with morning stiffness, older age, fatigue, headache or jaw pain on chewing
Refer same day if vision or headache involved

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Recent trauma, seizure or shock with locked rotation? **Yes:** refer urgently.
Passive external rotation clearly reduced in a capsular pattern, with pain and normal or non-explaining X-ray? **Yes:** working diagnosis is adhesive capsulitis.
Decide the phase from pain, night pain and stiffness.
If irritable and painful: calm first. If stiff and less painful: more active stretching.
If no progress or severe disability after months of care: medical review for injection or procedure options.

rows: Short-term pain relief without forcing range
Irritable shoulder, high pain, night pain
Supine, gentle oscillations in pain-free range, below the first resistance
Graded mobilization to the end of range (stiff phase)
Moderate-grade glides toward limited directions such as external rotation; short bouts
Pain over about 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and symptom-guided gentle movement. Avoid aggressive stretching or forced end-range manipulation in the painful phase, because it can increase pain and may delay recovery [Ref - to verify]. The evidence for manual therapy in frozen shoulder is limited and mostly low in certainty [Ref - to verify]. Do not claim that mobilization breaks adhesions.
**Is it working?** Compare passive external rotation, night pain and function over weeks, not minutes. Natural recovery makes short-term judgments difficult.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Lean forward with support, let the arm hang and swing gently
1 to 2 minutes, a few times daily
Supine stick or towel external rotation
Lying, elbow at the side, push the hand outward with the other arm holding a stick
Seated, hands on a table, slide forward
Face the wall, walk fingers up

blocks.text: **Dose idea:** in the painful phase, use short, gentle, frequent movements below the pain threshold. In the stiff phase, use longer holds at the end of the available range, with mild to moderate stretch discomfort that eases within an hour [Ref - to verify].

rows: Evidence limited and mixed [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: **Medical options (decided by doctors):** intra-articular corticosteroid injection, especially in the painful phase, which is reported to give short-term pain relief and some improvement in range [Ref - to verify]; hydrodilatation; manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release for severe stiffness that does not improve. Timing is individual.

items: **Visit 1:** confirm the diagnosis and phase, screen flags, explain the usual course and that it improves with time.
**Painful phase:** pain control, sleep positioning, gentle movement, consider medical advice on injection.
**Stiff phase:** progress stretching and strengthening; add functional range tasks.
**Thawing:** restore strength, normalise movement and return to full activity.
**If no progress after many months of regular care or severe disability:** discuss procedures with the doctor.

blocks.text: Record pain scale, night pain, passive external rotation, passive abduction, hand-behind-back reach, and a shoulder questionnaire such as SPADI [Ref - to verify].

rows: Pain lower, range stable or better
No change after many months, severe limitation
Sudden new weakness or locked joint

blocks.text: **Case:** A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has 3 months of worsening left shoulder pain, worst at night, and cannot reach behind her back or comb her hair. Passive external rotation at the side is about 15 degrees on the left and 70 on the right. Passive abduction is also limited. Strength is normal apart from pain. X-ray is reported as normal.

**Working diagnosis:** adhesive capsulitis, probably in the freezing (painful) phase. **Plan:** education, gentle pain-guided mobility, sleep positioning, low-grade mobilization, discuss injection with the doctor, and a diabetes review with her doctor.
**Questions and answers**

items: How do you separate frozen shoulder from a cuff problem on examination? Passive movement is limited in frozen shoulder, especially external rotation, whereas in cuff problems passive range is usually normal and the limit is pain on active movement.
Why avoid aggressive stretching in the painful phase? It may increase pain and inflammation and make the shoulder more irritable [Ref - to verify].
Why ask about a seizure or electric shock? These can cause a locked posterior dislocation that looks like a stiff shoulder and needs urgent imaging.
Why mention diabetes? It is a common association and may need medical review; blood sugar control may also matter [Ref - to verify].

The patient asks how long it will last. What do you say? Explain that the course is variable, from many months to a few years, with most people improving, and that treatment aims to reduce pain and keep as much function as possible [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** education, pain control and symptom-guided movement.
**Justifying findings:** painful stiff shoulder, reduced passive range with external rotation worst, no trauma or red flags.
**Priority:** match treatment to phase.
**Manual therapy:** gentle in the painful phase; graded stretching in the stiff phase.
**Exercise:** pendulum, assisted external rotation, wall walks, light strengthening.
**Modalities:** optional comfort only.
**Tell the patient:** it is self-limiting for most people but slow; movement still matters.
**Avoid:** forced stretching, complete immobilisation, promising a quick fix.
**Measure:** passive external rotation, pain, night pain, SPADI.
**If no improvement:** medical review for injection or procedure.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** function restored enough for daily tasks, patient able to self-manage.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no trauma, normal X-ray, no systemic red flags.

items: **Can be tested:** whether injection, exercise or mobilization improves pain and range compared with natural recovery.
**Hypotheses:** that capsule inflammation is the key driver; that stretching dose affects outcome.
**Future questions:** best timing of injection and exercise by phase.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.
